findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch to Git without invoking a shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, such as `main; arbitrary-command`, `exec()` interprets it and runs the injected command with the process's privileges. Shell metacharacters can also cause legitimate branch values to be parsed incorrectly. Preserve the previous argument-array invocation or otherwise avoid shell interpolation.

findings.title: [P1] Preserve branch names as a single argument
findings.body:
On POSIX systems, `exec` invokes `/bin/sh`, so valid Git ref characters become shell syntax. For an existing branch named `topic;true`, this runs `git show topic` followed by `true` instead of showing `topic;true`; the returned process then reports exit code 0 even if `git show topic` failed. This corrupts command ordering and completion state and can execute arbitrary commands when branch input is externally controlled.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Keep cancellation targeted at the Git process
findings.body:
`exec` returns the intermediary shell process rather than the directly spawned Git process. On POSIX systems, calling `.kill()` on the returned child during a long-running `git show` can terminate only the shell while its Git child continues running and retaining pipes/resources. Previously, `execFile` made cancellation target Git directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the command shell
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` verbatim. If the branch value is attacker-controlled, input such as `main; touch /tmp/pwned` executes arbitrary commands with the process’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` call passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
